definition: Tracing directly over filmed live-action footage or a rendered CG model, frame by frame, to produce the final drawn animation — a stronger, more literal practice than merely watching reference for timing: the traced footage IS the motion, redrawn at proportions that differ from the reference performer's own.
purpose: Achieve fluid, well-choreographed motion (especially for complex fight choreography) that would be very hard to key from imagination alone, by capturing a real performance's actual movement and translating it into the drawn character's different proportions.
visible_effect: Drawn character motion whose timing, weight-shift and spacing tracks a real filmed performance closely — confirmed in this session's frames showing the source's own filmed choreography reference (two performers with motion-capture-style markers on a gridded floor, t=03:32) directly adjacent to the resulting anime cut.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Done well, reads as unusually fluid and well-choreographed motion; done under time pressure, reads as 'uncanny' or 'too realistic' in a way some viewers dislike, per the source's own stated criticism some animators receive.
physical_interpretation: A direct capture-and-redraw of real human motion, not an invented or exaggerated pose sequence — the closest thing in this batch's 2D-only sources to Cadence's own Roblox-Studio-Animation-Capture pipeline for 3D.
use_cases: complex fight choreography that benefits from a real, physically-blocked performance (the source's named example: a schoolgirl action series using it heavily so its fights read as fluid and well-choreographed)
any motion an animator would otherwise struggle to key convincingly from imagination alone
non_use_cases: a production without enough schedule to finish the rotoscoped work properly — the source states directly that an incomplete/rushed rotoscope pass 'can look bad'

a character whose proportions differ drastically from any available performer, where the source notes real translation work (redrawing hair, build, proportions) is still required and is nontrivial — rotoscoping is not a shortcut past drawing skill
interactions: physical_reference_timing_method (W01, v9) — that entry is filmed reference informing TIMING/spacing decisions the animator then keys by hand; this entry is the more literal practice of tracing the reference footage itself frame-by-frame, a stronger dependency on the source performance

REF-001 / Roblox Studio Animation Capture (per this program's LEARNING_LOOP_PROMPT) — Cadence's own closest equivalent: Studio's Animation Capture estimates R15 keyframes directly from video, the same 'trace real motion onto a different-proportioned character' structure this entry describes, and is subject to the same proportion-mismatch caveat this entry raises for hand-rotoscoping

style_variations.anime: an established, named production technique with both respected practitioners and known failure cases per the source
style_variations.realistic: not applicable as a distinct technique — rotoscoping IS the realistic-motion route by construction

cadence_representation: Not directly representable as a 2D drawing process, but its underlying idea — deriving keyframes from real filmed motion rather than authoring them by hand — is exactly what Roblox Studio's Animation Capture already does for this project's own pipeline (per `docs/animation-intelligence/LEARNING_LOOP_PROMPT.md`), with the same proportion-translation caveat this entry's non_use_cases raises: a captured/rotoscoped clip must be re-targeted to the receiving rig's own proportions, never assumed to transfer 1:1.
control_surface: `import_from_studio` + `add_to_library` (provenance `captured`, `estimated: true`) is Cadence's reachable equivalent pipeline stage.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not measurable in this build as a 2D production technique; the CAPTURED-clip analogue is already governed by `add_to_library`'s existing estimated/licence validation rather than a new measurement.
generation_or_modification_methods: None directly (2D drawing process); the 3D analogue's generation path is Roblox Studio's Animation Capture, already documented elsewhere in this programme.
failure_modes: an incomplete or rushed rotoscope pass reading as choppy or unfinished, per the source's own named example
reading as uncannily realistic in a way that clashes with a stylized production's established look, per the source's own stated criticism some rotoscoped work receives
assuming the reference performer's proportions transfer directly to the drawn character without translation work, which the source states is still required and nontrivial
roblox_considerations: Directly analogous to Roblox Studio's Animation Capture (Body/Face) pipeline already documented in this programme: a captured clip is a pose ESTIMATE that must be retargeted to the R15 rig's own proportions and stays labelled `estimated: true`, never presented as exact.
performance_implications: Not applicable to a 2D production technique; the 3D analogue's cost is the Animation Capture process itself, already characterized elsewhere (~1 minute to process a short clip).
examples: 'rotoscoping is basically tracing over live-action footage or CG models... you still need talent to trace the live-action footage to anime because the proportions are different' (video @ 03:27–04:00), confirmed in this session's frame at t=03:32 showing the source's own filmed choreography reference (two performers, markers, gridded floor) beside the anime result

'a good example for live-action rotoscoping use... they use a lot of them so that the fights look more fluid and the choreography is better... but if you don't have time to finish the work, rotoscoping can look bad' (video @ 04:21–04:35)
